Pau Brasil is named among the trees of the evergreen rainforests of Brazil. Teak is named among the trees of the deciduous forests, which shed their leaves in the dry season. The coastal forests of swampy areas, estuaries and lagoons are the mangroves, called Sunderbans in India, after the Sundar trees. Pine is one of the coniferous trees found at medium altitude in the Indian Himalayas, along with deodar and fir. Khejadi is named among the thorny and shrub-type vegetation of regions receiving less than 500 mm of rainfall.

Items (vi) Orchid and (vii) Sal are left over: orchids are named among the vegetation of Brazil and sal among the mixed forests at the Himalayan foothills, but the printed column A has only five entries for column B's seven.

Both countries owe their forest types to rainfall, but the range of types differs.

Brazil has the largest number of vegetation species in the world, including evergreen, semi-evergreen and arid types. In most parts of the equatorial region it rains throughout the year, so equatorial and tropical evergreen forests cover the Amazon basin, with trees like Pau Brasil, rubber, mahogany, rosewood and a variety of orchids. Moving away from the equator the rainy days and the rainfall reduce, so deciduous forests, then grassland and finally temperate forests appear towards the south.

India has five types set by rainfall and by altitude. Evergreen forests grow where rainfall is more than 2000 mm with abundant sunlight; their trees are broad-leaved with hardwood that is heavy and durable, such as mahogany, rosewood and rubber, and biodiversity is highest there. Deciduous forests grow between 1000 mm and 2000 mm and shed their leaves in the dry season so that water is not lost by evaporation — teak, bamboo, banyan and peepal. Thorny and shrub-type vegetation with small leaves grows below 500 mm — catechu, acacia, khejadi and cacti like aloe vera and agave. Coastal or mangrove vegetation, called the Sunderbans, grows in swampy areas, estuaries and lagoons with saline soils, and its wood is oily, light and durable. And the Indian Himalayas carry three types by altitude: seasonally flowering trees at the highest altitudes, coniferous trees such as pine, deodar and fir at medium altitudes, and mixed forests with a higher proportion of sal at the foothills.

The chief difference is that India has Himalayan forests and mangrove forests, which Brazil does not, while Brazil's equatorial forests cover a far greater area than any evergreen forest in India.

Wildlife lives where the vegetation suits it, so the animals of each region follow the forest type.

In Brazil the swampy areas of the Pantanal hold huge anacondas; the forests hold guinea pigs, crocodiles, alligators, monkeys, pumas and leopards; the rivers hold pink dolphins and piranhas while swordfish are found in the seas; and condors, parrots, macaws and flamingoes are the major birds. Millions of insect varieties are also found there. Figure 5.2 shows the same correlation as a cross profile: apes and reptiles with the equatorial forests, arboreal and aquatic animals with the tropical forests, and grassland animals where the grasslands are.

In India the same rule holds. Elephants are found in hot and humid forests; one-horned rhinoceroses in the swampy and marshy lands of Assam; wild ass and camels in arid lands; snow leopards and yaks in the snow-capped regions of the Himalayas; and Indian bison, deer, antelopes and monkeys in the Peninsular region. Rivers, estuaries and coastal areas are the homes of turtles, crocodiles and gavials, and the forests and wetlands shelter peacocks, Indian bustard, kingfishers, pheasants, ducks, parakeets, cranes and pigeons.

India is the only country in the world where both tigers and lions are found, and Brazil has a greater diversity of wildlife than any other country — in each case because the country's range of vegetation is itself wide.

Both countries face the loss of their forests and their wildlife.

In Brazil the environment is being degraded by the illegal smuggling of wild animals, by slash and burn agriculture — the shifting cultivation called Roca, in which land under forest is cleared by cutting and burning — by deforestation and by pollution. Many endemic species are on the verge of extinction because of these. A survey done in 2016 found that approximately 5831 sq. km of land under forests in Brazil had already degraded in that year alone.

In India many species of wildlife are on the verge of extinction because of poaching, pollution and rapidly occurring deforestation; the chapter gives cheetahs as an example.

So the issues are shared: deforestation, pollution, and the loss of species — with poaching in India and the smuggling of wild animals in Brazil.

In Brazil the major causes named by the chapter are slash and burn agriculture, deforestation and pollution. The slash and burn method is the shifting agriculture called Roca, in which the land under forests is cleared by cutting and burning and subsistence agriculture is then followed on that patch for the next few years. Illegal smuggling of wild animals adds to the degradation. The scale is large: about 5831 sq. km of forest land in Brazil degraded in 2016 alone.

In India the major causes are rapidly occurring deforestation, pollution and poaching.

Deforestation and pollution are therefore common to both, and each country adds one of its own — the Roca method of clearing in Brazil, and poaching in India.

The type of vegetation of a region is set chiefly by how much rain it gets, and deciduous forests are the type suited to rainfall between 1000 mm and 2000 mm.

Most of India receives rainfall in that range. Evergreen forests need more than 2000 mm along with abundant sunlight, and those conditions are met only in limited areas; thorny and shrub-type vegetation belongs to regions with less than 500 mm and long dry summers, which again is only part of the north-west.

Deciduous trees are also well suited to India's monsoon climate, in which the rain falls in one season and a dry season follows: they shed their leaves in the dry season so that water is not lost by evaporation. That is why teak, bamboo, banyan and peepal forests occupy most of the country.

The equator passes through the northern part of Brazil, and in most parts of the equatorial region it rains throughout the year.

Evergreen forests are found exactly where it rains throughout the year, because the trees never lack the water they need and so never have to shed their leaves. The Amazon valley there receives around 2000 mm of rainfall and its average temperature is 25°–28° C, so warmth and moisture are both available all year.

That is why the northern part of Brazil is covered by dense evergreen rainforest — the forest the chapter calls the 'lungs of the world', because the oxygen it releases helps to reduce carbon dioxide levels.

In the Indian Himalayas three types of forest are found according to the altitude, and the vegetation thins as the altitude rises.

At the foothills there are mixed forests, both coniferous and deciduous, in which the proportion of sal trees is higher. In regions of medium altitude there are coniferous trees such as pine, deodar and fir. In the areas located at the highest altitude only seasonally flowering trees are found.

The reason is that the growing conditions get harder as one climbs. Figure 5.3 shows the highest part of the north as Cold Desert, and the chapter's own question about these forests calls that region snow-capped. Where the ground is snow-covered and the season for growth is short, trees cannot establish themselves, so vegetation there is scarce and only the hardiest, seasonally flowering plants survive.

Brazil has the largest number of vegetation species in the world and a greater diversity of wildlife than any other country, and insects share in that.

The reason is the equatorial forest. Over most of the equatorial region of Brazil it rains throughout the year and the temperature stays between 25° and 28° C, so the evergreen rainforest grows continuously and offers food and shelter at every level of the forest all year round, without a cold or a dry season to interrupt it.

Because that habitat is so large and so unbroken, millions of insect varieties are found there.

Many species of wildlife are on the verge of extinction from India because of poaching, pollution and rapidly occurring deforestation; the chapter gives the cheetah as an example.

Deforestation destroys the habitat an animal needs — the chapter's own account of Indian wildlife shows how closely each species is tied to one kind of country, elephants to hot and humid forests, one-horned rhinoceroses to the marshes of Assam, snow leopards and yaks to the snow-capped Himalayas. Poaching kills the animals directly, and pollution makes the rivers, estuaries and coastal areas that shelter turtles, crocodiles and gavials unfit for them.

Because all three are at work together, wildlife in India is decreasing day by day. To meet this the Government of India has set up a number of national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, bird sanctuaries and biosphere reserves for the protection of wildlife and forests.

Brazil's forests are being lost at a great rate — about 5831 sq. km of land under forest degraded in 2016 alone — through slash and burn agriculture (Roca), deforestation, pollution and the illegal smuggling of wild animals. Many endemic species are on the verge of extinction as a result.

What is lost matters beyond Brazil. Because of its evergreen rainforests a large amount of oxygen is released into the environment, which helps to reduce carbon dioxide levels, and the chapter says these rainforests are rightly called the 'lungs of the world'. Brazil also has the largest number of vegetation species in the world and a greater diversity of wildlife than any other country.

India has met the same problem by setting up national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, bird sanctuaries and biosphere reserves. Since the causes in Brazil are the same and the consequences reach the whole world, there is need of conservation of forests in Brazil too.
